scenes.tts: A mouse reels as it walks. Is that a walking problem, or a building problem?
scenes.visual: Title card: Same Neurons, Wrong Order. A schematic mouse weaving from side to side.
scenes.narration: A mouse reels as it walks. Is that a walking problem, or a building problem?

scenes.tts: In nineteen fifty-one, Douglas Falconer named this mutant reeler. Its cortex was the deeper puzzle.
scenes.caption: In 1951, Douglas Falconer named this mutant reeler. Its cortex was the deeper puzzle.
scenes.visual: Credit: Falconer, 1951. A small cerebellum, then the view moves up to the cerebral cortex.
scenes.narration: In 1951, Douglas Falconer named this mutant reeler. Its cortex was the deeper puzzle.

scenes.tts: First, direction. Deep means near the ventricle, where neurons are born. Superficial means near the outer surface.
scenes.visual: A vertical cortex schematic, kept fixed for the chapter. Bottom labelled ventricle, deep. Top labelled pial surface, superficial.
scenes.narration: First, direction. Deep means near the ventricle, where neurons are born. Superficial means near the outer surface.

scenes.tts: The first neurons form a thin sheet under the surface, the preplate. The next neurons split it in two.
scenes.visual: Dark dots rise and form a thin sheet near the top (preplate). A lighter wave pushes into it and parts it.
scenes.narration: The first neurons form a thin sheet under the surface, the preplate. The next neurons split it in two.

scenes.tts: Above sits the marginal zone, with the Cajal-Retzius cells. Below sits the subplate.
scenes.visual: Labels: marginal zone (with Cajal-Retzius cells) on top; cortical plate in the middle; subplate below.
scenes.narration: Above sits the marginal zone, with the Cajal-Retzius cells. Below sits the subplate.

scenes.tts: Each later wave climbs past the waves before it, and settles just under the marginal zone.
scenes.visual: Later waves, each a lighter colour, climb to the top of the plate and settle just under the marginal zone. On-screen caption: Schematic: six illustrative birth cohorts.
scenes.narration: Each later wave climbs past the waves before it, and settles just under the marginal zone.

scenes.tts: So the cortex is built inside-out. Early-born neurons end up deep, and late-born neurons near the surface.
scenes.visual: The finished stack: darkest (earliest) at the bottom, lightest (latest) at the top. Label: inside-out.
scenes.narration: So the cortex is built inside-out. Early-born neurons end up deep, and late-born neurons near the surface.

scenes.tts: Is reeler making the wrong neurons, or putting the right ones in the wrong place?
scenes.visual: Split screen: normal stack on the left, a jumbled reeler stack on the right. Two question cards: wrong neurons? wrong place?
scenes.narration: Is reeler making the wrong neurons, or putting the right ones in the wrong place?

scenes.tts: Verne Caviness and Richard Sidman used birthdating. A radioactive building block of D N A labels cells copying their D N A.
scenes.caption: Verne Caviness and Richard Sidman used birthdating. A radioactive building block of DNA labels cells copying their DNA.
scenes.visual: Credit: Caviness and Sidman. A pulse of label (tritiated thymidine) enters cells that are copying DNA.
scenes.narration: Verne Caviness and Richard Sidman used birthdating. A radioactive building block of DNA labels cells copying their DNA.

scenes.tts: Each division shares the label between two daughter cells. A cell that divides once more, then never again, stays heavily labelled.
scenes.visual: A labelled progenitor divides: the label is split between its two daughters. Daughters that keep dividing fade by half each time; a daughter that stops dividing stays bright from then on. Its adult position marks where neurons born that day settle.
scenes.narration: Each division shares the label between two daughter cells. A cell that divides once more, then never again, stays heavily labelled.

scenes.tts: Predict. If reeler made the wrong neurons, what would birthdating show? And if it misplaced the right ones?
scenes.visual: Predict card over the split screen.
scenes.narration: Predict. If reeler made the wrong neurons, what would birthdating show? And if it misplaced the right ones?

scenes.tts: In nineteen seventy-three: the same classes of neurons, born on the same schedule.
scenes.caption: In 1973: the same classes of neurons, born on the same schedule.
scenes.visual: Credit: Caviness and Sidman, 1973. Both columns show the same six illustrative colours, born on the same days.
scenes.narration: In 1973: the same classes of neurons, born on the same schedule.

scenes.tts: What changed was their order. Early-born neurons tended to sit near the surface, and late-born neurons deep.
scenes.visual: The reeler column re-sorts: dark dots drift toward the top, light dots toward the bottom.
scenes.narration: What changed was their order. Early-born neurons tended to sit near the surface, and late-born neurons deep.

scenes.tts: The pattern was roughly inverted, with a lot of scatter.
scenes.visual: Many dots out of place. Label: roughly inverted, not a mirror image.
scenes.narration: The pattern was roughly inverted, with a lot of scatter.

scenes.tts: Why? In reeler, the preplate fails to split. Later waves tend to stop beneath the neurons already there.
scenes.visual: Replay in reeler: the second wave stalls under an unsplit sheet, labelled superplate. Later waves stop below the earlier ones.
scenes.narration: Why? In reeler, the preplate fails to split. Later waves tend to stop beneath the neurons already there.

scenes.tts: So reeler is a defect of placement, not production. The missing protein, Reelin, is needed to stack that birth order the right way up.
scenes.visual: Guiding idea card: Neurons are born in order; Reelin signalling is needed to stack that order the right way up.
scenes.narration: So reeler is a defect of placement, not production. The missing protein, Reelin, is needed to stack that birth order the right way up.

scenes.tts: With Reelin signalling, each new wave tends to finish its climb at the top. Without it, newcomers tend to stop beneath their elders.
scenes.visual: Two short animations side by side, each with a wave of several newcomers: on the left most climb to the top of the cortical plate; on the right most stop beneath the older neurons, with some scatter.
scenes.narration: With Reelin signalling, each new wave tends to finish its climb at the top. Without it, newcomers tend to stop beneath their elders.

scenes.tts: Takeaway: made on schedule, stacked the wrong way up. Next, where does Reelin come from?
scenes.visual: Closing card: made on schedule, stacked the wrong way up. Teaser: where does Reelin come from?
scenes.narration: Takeaway: made on schedule, stacked the wrong way up. Next, where does Reelin come from?
